seed: I want to make a video about why systems beat hustle. Everyone in my world thinks the answer to being slammed is to wake up earlier and grind harder. That is the trap. I worked 80 hour weeks for two years and my business did not grow, It stayed the same while making me a worse overall person. What actually changed was that I built a system for client onboarding. I realized that I was doing the same thing over and over again, and I needed to start to build systems. I want to show people that the goal is not to do more, the goal is to build the thing that does it for you.

reveals: The onboarding system is the one I always point to. I had a client, Marcus, who cut his onboarding from 5 hours per client down to 1 hour just by writing the steps down and handing them off.
I like the restaurant kitchen comparison. A good kitchen runs because every station knows its job, not because the chef is faster than everyone else.
The payoff for the viewer is they pick one repeatable task this week and write the steps down so someone else can run it.

distinctive_phrases: it stayed the same while making me a worse overall person
the goal is to build the thing that does it for you

seed: I want to do a video on a client win. Marcus ran a small agency and he was the bottleneck on everything. Nothing shipped unless he touched it. We spent six weeks pulling the onboarding out of his head and into a documented system, and he handed it to his coordinator. He cut his own onboarding time from 5 hours to 1 hour and he stopped being the bottleneck. The teaching point is that delegation is not about trust, it is about documentation.

reveals: Marcus is a real client, he runs a content agency. I already have his story and the proof screenshot in my banks.
The shift was when he realized he was not the only one who could do the work, he was just the only one with the steps in his head.
Viewer outcome: pick the one task only you can do right now and document it so it is no longer only you.

seed: Here are my notes for a listicle on onboarding mistakes. 1. No written steps, it all lives in your head. 2. Onboarding the client and onboarding your team are treated as the same thing. 3. No owner assigned to the process. 4. You document it once and never update it. 5. You measure nothing so you cannot tell if it is working. I want each one to have a quick example.

reveals: Mistake one is the big one, it ties back to the documentation point I always make.
For the example on mistake three, the Marcus story fits, he had a process but no owner so it defaulted back to him.
Viewer outcome: audit their own onboarding against these five and fix the first one that is broken.

distinctive_phrases: it all lives in your head
you measure nothing so you cannot tell if it is working
